reading.passage: Psychological resilience—the capacity to adapt successfully to adversity, trauma, or significant stress—has gained substantial attention in behavioral science. Far from being an innate trait possessed by a fortunate few, resilience involves behaviors, thoughts, and actions that can be learned and developed over time. Key factors contributing to psychological resilience include strong interpersonal relationships, emotional self-regulation, realistic goal setting, and cognitive reframing. Cognitive reframing allows individuals to view stressful circumstances as manageable challenges rather than insurmountable obstacles.

reading.passage: Epistemological discourse in post-modern philosophy frequently interrogates the foundationalist premise that objective truth can be apprehended independently of socio-linguistic constructs. Proponents of radical constructivism contend that reality is not an external realm waiting to be discovered, but rather an ongoing narrative forged through discursive practices and cultural paradigms. Critics, however, argue that relinquishing the concept of an objective reality risks slipping into moral and intellectual relativism, thereby undermining the scientific method and eroding the philosophical underpinnings of universal human rights.
